concepts.title: rabbit mq.docx
concepts.content:
What is RabbitMQ?
RabbitMQ is an open-source Message Broker. It acts as a digital post office or middleware layer that allows different applications, servers, or microservices to talk to each other and pass data safely without being directly connected. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] 
It implements the AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) standard. Instead of Service A calling Service B over a direct HTTP connection, Service A drops a message into RabbitMQ, and RabbitMQ ensures that message is reliably routed and delivered to Service B when it is ready. [6, 7, 8, 9] 
Key Concepts: How It Works
Producer: The application that sends the message (e.g., your FastAPI backend).
Queue: A buffer inside RabbitMQ that holds messages sequentially until they are processed.
Consumer: The application that waits for messages from the queue and processes them (e.g., your ML Model Worker).
Exchange: The routing brain. Producers send messages to an Exchange, which looks at routing rules (routing keys) and decides exactly which Queue the message should land in. [10, 11, 12, 13, 14] 
Where is RabbitMQ Used? (Key Use Cases)
RabbitMQ excels in architectures that require complex routing, bulletproof reliability, and asynchronous task handling. [15, 16, 17] 
1. Long-Running Background Tasks (Asynchronous Processing) [18, 19, 20] 
If a user triggers an action that takes a long time, you don't make them wait on a loading screen. [21] 
Example: When a user orders food on an app, the checkout service drops a "Generate PDF Invoice" message into RabbitMQ and immediately tells the user "Order Placed!". A background worker pulls that message from RabbitMQ and compiles the PDF without slowing down the user. [22, 23, 24, 25] 
2. Complex Routing and Workflows [26] 
RabbitMQ has advanced exchange patterns (Direct, Fanout, Topic, Headers) that let you split or broadcast messages based on metadata. [27, 28, 29, 30, 31] 
Example: An inventory update message enters a RabbitMQ exchange. RabbitMQ automatically forwards that exact same message to three different queues simultaneously: the Analytics Queue, the Email Notification Queue, and the Warehouse Update Queue. [32, 33] 
3. Decoupling Microservices
In microservice architectures, you don't want a crash in one system to crash your entire company. If Service B goes down for maintenance, RabbitMQ will safely store all messages meant for Service B in its queue. When Service B comes back online, it picks up exactly where it left off without losing a single data point. [34, 35, 36] 
4. Financial Systems & Order Fulfillment
Unlike standard in-memory caches, RabbitMQ is built for message durability. It ensures messages are written to disk and requires acknowledgment (ACKs) from consumers. If a worker crashes halfway through processing an order, RabbitMQ detects the failure and re-queues the message so another worker can complete it. [37, 38, 39, 40, 41] 
RabbitMQ vs. Redis vs. Kafka (Quick Reference)
Since you are working with Kafka and Redis, it helps to understand exactly where RabbitMQ sits: [42] 
Would you like to know how RabbitMQ's message acknowledgement system compares to Kafka's offset tracking, or are you looking to see if RabbitMQ could replace Kafka in your specific UPI project?
How RabbitMQ Compares to Kafka (Similarities & Critical Differences)
Yes, at a high level, they serve a similar purpose: moving data asynchronously between parts of an application. However, how they handle that data internally is fundamentally different. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] 
Think of RabbitMQ as a Post Office and Kafka as a Continuous Audio Recorder. [6, 7, 8] 
1. Message Retention (The Biggest Difference)
RabbitMQ (Transient Queue): Once a consumer pulls a transaction message, processes it, and sends back an acknowledgment (ACK), RabbitMQ permanently deletes that message from its memory/disk. The queue naturally drains to zero. [9, 10, 11, 12] 
Kafka (Log-Based): Kafka does not delete messages after they are read. It appends transactions to a continuous log file on disk and keeps them for a set duration (e.g., 7 days). [13, 14, 15, 16, 17] 
2. Tracking Consumption (ACKs vs. Offsets)
RabbitMQ uses Acknowledgements (ACKs): RabbitMQ hands a message to a worker. It keeps track of that specific individual message. If the worker crashes before sending an "ACK", RabbitMQ puts that specific message back at the front of the line. [18, 19, 20, 21, 22] 
Kafka uses Offsets: Because Kafka doesn't delete messages, it doesn't track individual delivery status. Instead, it uses a pointer called an Offset (e.g., "Worker 1 has read up to message #405"). If Worker 1 crashes and restarts, it checks the offset log and continues reading from message #406. [23, 24, 25, 26, 27] 
Can you use RabbitMQ for your UPI project?
Yes. Instead of pushing your transaction burst from FastAPI into Kafka, you can push it to a RabbitMQ queue, and your ML workers can pull from it. For a project demo, the behavior will look almost identical on screen.
How to Use RabbitMQ for Free
Just like Redis, RabbitMQ is open-source and free. You can host it yourself locally or use a free managed cloud instance. [28, 29, 30, 31, 32] 
Option A: Serverless Cloud Free Tier (Recommended for Your Project)
If you don't want to install anything on your machine, use a managed provider that handles the setup for you and gives you an instant AMQP connection string URL.
Platform: CloudAMQP
The Plan: Their "Little Lemur" plan is 100% free forever. It gives you a fully managed RabbitMQ cluster capable of handling up to 1 million messages per month, which is more than enough to test your ML models and demo your UPI app. [33, 34] 
Option B: Local Docker Container (Best for Offline Dev)
If you want to run massive throughput tests on your local laptop without internet latency or cloud data limits, spin it up using Docker:
Open your terminal.
Run this single command:
docker run -d --name local-rabbitmq -p 5672:5672 -p 15672:15672 rabbitmq:3-management
The Bonus: Open your browser and go to http://localhost:15672. Log in with username guest and password guest. This opens the RabbitMQ Management Dashboard, a free visual UI where you can watch your queues grow, shrink, and track messages in real time during your demo. [35, 36, 37, 38, 39] 
Quick Python Code: Replacing Kafka with Free RabbitMQ
To interact with RabbitMQ in Python, you use a library called pika. You can install it via pip install pika. [40, 41] 
Here is how you would send a UPI transaction to your free RabbitMQ instance:
import pika
import json
# 1. Connect to RabbitMQ (Replace localhost with your CloudAMQP URL if using the cloud)
connection = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.ConnectionParameters(host='localhost'))
channel = connection.channel()
# 2. Declare a queue (This creates it if it doesn't exist yet)
channel.queue_declare(queue='upi_fraud_queue', durable=True)
# 3. Create a mock UPI transaction
upi_payload = {
    "transaction_id": "TXN987654",
    "sender_upi_id": "rahul@okaxis",
    "amount": 15000.00
}
# 4. Publish the message to the queue
channel.basic_publish(
    exchange='',
    routing_key='upi_fraud_queue',
    body=json.dumps(upi_payload),
    properties=pika.BasicProperties(
        delivery_mode=2,  # Makes the message durable (saves to disk so it survives broker crashes)
    )
)
print(" [x] Sent UPI transaction to RabbitMQ!")
connection.close()
Would you like to see how to write the accompanying Consumer script that pulls this payload out of RabbitMQ and passes it to your ML model pipeline?

concepts.title: redis.docx
concepts.content:
Why Redis is Essential for UPI Fraud Detection
Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions must resolve in milliseconds. Machine Learning (ML) models are notoriously slow when they have to fetch raw transaction history from a disk database (like PostgreSQL) to compute risk features (e.g., “How many transactions did this user make in the last 10 minutes?”). [1] 
Redis solves this by acting as a high-speed, in-memory Feature Store and Inference Cache. It stores live transaction metrics in RAM, allowing your ML models to fetch inputs instantly and flag fraud before the UPI transaction completes. [2, 3, 4] 
Step 1: Choose Your Platform & Infrastructure
You have two main paths depending on whether you want a zero-maintenance cloud or complete control over your system:
Option A: Serverless Cloud (Recommended for Projects)
Platform: Upstash Redis or Redis Cloud Free Tier
Why: They offer a generous 100% free tier that requires zero installation. They give you a connection string URL instantly.
Best for: Fast deployment, prototyping, and integrating directly into FastAPI serverless setups. [5, 6]

Step 2: The Architecture Design (How it Fits Together)
Your system will utilize a hybrid data-driven pipeline combining FastAPI, Redis, and your ML models.
[UPI Transaction Request] ──> [FastAPI Endpoint]
                                   │
       ┌───────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┐
       ▼                                                       ▼
[Fetch Real-Time Features]                                [Inference Cache]
 (Redis Hashes / Sorted Sets)                             (Check if same payload 
       │                                                   was evaluated recently)
       ▼                                                       │
[Feed Array to ML Models] <────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
[Return Fraud Score (0 or 1)]
The Request: FastAPI intercepts the incoming UPI payload (Sender, Receiver, Amount, Timestamp).
Feature Enrichment: FastAPI pulls historical context from Redis (e.g., sender's average transaction amount, velocity count) in microseconds.
Inference: The combined features are passed into your pre-loaded ML models (e.g., XGBoost, Scikit-Learn).
Update: The current transaction data is written back to Redis to update the user's velocity metrics for the next transaction. [7, 8, 9, 10, 11] 
Step 3: Complete Python Implementation Code
This complete, production-ready pipeline demonstrates how to use Redis Hashes for user profiles and Redis Sorted Sets (ZSETs) to compute real-time transaction sliding windows (velocity checking).
import time
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel
import redis
import numpy as np
app = FastAPI(title="UPI Fraud Detection System")
# 1. CONNECT TO REDIS
# For local Docker use localhost. For Upstash/Redis Cloud, paste your rediss:// URL here.
r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, decode_responses=True)
# 2. DATA SCHEMAS
class UPITransaction(BaseModel):
    transaction_id: str
    sender_upi_id: str
    receiver_upi_id: str
    amount: float
# Mock ML Model (Replace this with your joblib.load("model.pkl") system)
class MockFraudModel:
    def predict_proba(self, features: list):
        # Expecting features: [amount, tx_count_last_10m, avg_historical_amount]
        amount, tx_count, avg_amount = features[0]
        # Simple rule-based mock logic resembling an ML decision tree boundary
        score = 0.1
        if tx_count > 5: score += 0.4  # High frequency velocity burst
        if amount > (avg_amount * 3) and avg_amount > 0: score += 0.4  # Sudden massive spike
        return np.array([[1 - score, score]])
ml_model = MockFraudModel()
# 3. FASTAPI ROUTE WITH INTEGRATED REDIS FEATURE STORE
@app.post("/v1/check-fraud")
async def check_fraud(tx: UPITransaction):
    current_time = time.time()
    ten_minutes_ago = current_time - 600
    # ─── REDIS OPERATION 1: FEATURE ENRICHMENT (SLIDING WINDOW VELOCITY) ───
    # We use a Sorted Set (ZSET) where the score is the timestamp.
    user_history_key = f"user:tx_times:{tx.sender_upi_id}"
    # Add current transaction timestamp to the sorted set
    r.zadd(user_history_key, {tx.transaction_id: current_time})
    # Clear out timestamps older than 10 minutes to save RAM and keep window accurate
    r.zremrangebyscore(user_history_key, "-inf", ten_minutes_ago)
    # Count how many transactions occurred in the last 10 minutes
    tx_count_last_10m = r.zcard(user_history_key)
    # ─── REDIS OPERATION 2: PROFILE HISTORICAL METRICS ───
    # We use a Hash map to fetch pre-calculated historical trends
    profile_key = f"user:profile:{tx.sender_upi_id}"
    user_profile = r.hgetall(profile_key)
    # Fallback default values if this is a brand new user missing a profile
    avg_historical_amount = float(user_profile.get("avg_amount", 500.0))
    total_tx_completed = int(user_profile.get("total_tx", 1))
    # ─── EXECUTE ML INFERENCE ───
    # Construct feature vector dynamically using Redis data
    feature_vector = [[tx.amount, tx_count_last_10m, avg_historical_amount]]
    # Run the model pipeline
    probabilities = ml_model.predict_proba(feature_vector)
    fraud_probability = probabilities[0][1]
    is_fraud = bool(fraud_probability > 0.5)
    # ─── REDIS OPERATION 3: BACKGROUND PROFILE UPDATE ───
    # Recalculate historical average running metrics instantly in memory
    new_total_tx = total_tx_completed + 1
    new_avg_amount = ((avg_historical_amount * total_tx_completed) + tx.amount) / new_total_tx
    r.hset(profile_key, mapping={
        "avg_amount": str(new_avg_amount),
        "total_tx": str(new_total_tx)
    })
    # Optional: Expire user profile cache after 30 days of inactivity to preserve memory
    r.expire(profile_key, 2592000)
    # 4. RESPONSE OUTCOME
    return {
        "transaction_id": tx.transaction_id,
        "fraud_score": round(fraud_probability, 4),
        "action": "BLOCK" if is_fraud else "ALLOW",
        "enriched_features_used": {
            "tx_count_last_10m": tx_count_last_10m,
            "avg_historical_amount": round(avg_historical_amount, 2)
        }
    }

When processing high-throughput UPI transactions from Apache Kafka, your system can bottleneck if FastAPI tries to run heavy ML model inference for every single incoming message sequentially. [1] 
To handle a massive stream of transactions smoothly during your demo, Redis must act as a buffer queue and an evaluation cache between Kafka and your ML models. This architectural pattern is called the Stream-Worker Pattern.
The Architecture Design
Instead of making FastAPI process the transactions instantly, Kafka drops transactions into the system, FastAPI immediately pushes them into a Redis List (acting as a FIFO queue), and independent Background Workers pull from Redis to run the ML models.
[Massive Kafka Stream] 
        │
        ▼
 [FastAPI Consumer] ──(Microseconds)──> [Redis FIFO Queue] (List / Stream)
                                              │
                       ┌──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┐
                       ▼                                             ▼
               [Worker 1 (ML)]                               [Worker 2 (ML)]
         (Pulls batches from Redis)                    (Pulls batches from Redis)
                       │                                             │
                       └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                                              ▼
                                 [Write Fraud Flag to DB]
Why Use Redis Along with Kafka?
Decoupling Rate of Consumption: Kafka can blast 10,000 transactions per second. FastAPI can offload them to Redis instantly. Your ML workers can then process them at their own pace (e.g., 500 transactions per second) without crashing the system or missing transactions. [2] 
Easy Batching: Workers can pull transactions from Redis in batches of 32 or 64. ML frameworks (like Scikit-Learn or XGBoost) run significantly faster when processing matrix arrays in batches rather than looping one by one.
Complete Python Demo Setup
This script sets up a background processor using Python's multiprocessing or standard loop to mimic how workers pull from a Redis Queue using atomic brpop (blocking right pop) commands.
import json
import time
from fastapi import FastAPI, BackgroundTasks
from pydantic import BaseModel
import redis
import numpy as np
app = FastAPI(title="Kafka-Redis High Throughput UPI Fraud Pipeline")
# Connect to your local or cloud Redis instance
r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, decode_responses=True)
# Define the Redis key naming structures
QUEUE_KEY = "upi:transaction:queue"
CACHE_PREFIX = "upi:cache:"
class UPITransaction(BaseModel):
    transaction_id: str
    sender_upi_id: str
    receiver_upi_id: str
    amount: float
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. THE INGESTION LAYER (FastAPI consuming from Kafka simulation)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
@app.post("/v1/ingest-from-kafka")
async def ingest_transaction(tx: UPITransaction, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    """
    Imagine this route is triggered inside your Kafka consumer loop.
    Instead of running the ML model here, we push to Redis in microseconds.
    """
    tx_data = tx.model_dump()
    tx_data["ingested_at"] = time.time()
    # Check Inference Cache first: Has this specific sender sent this exact amount in last 2 seconds?
    # This deduplicates accidental double-taps or script floods before hitting ML models.
    cache_key = f"{CACHE_PREFIX}{tx.sender_upi_id}:{int(tx.amount)}"
    if r.get(cache_key):
        return {"transaction_id": tx.transaction_id, "status": "DUPLICATE_SUSPECT_BLOCKED"}
    # Set a temporary 2-second rate-limit cache block
    r.setex(cache_key, 2, "active")
    # Push into Redis List Queue (Left Push)
    r.lpush(QUEUE_KEY, json.dumps(tx_data))
    return {"transaction_id": tx.transaction_id, "status": "QUEUED_FOR_ML_INFERENCE"}
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. THE BACKGROUND PROCESSING WORKER (The ML Consumer)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def run_ml_worker():
    """
    Run this function in a separate terminal script or background process thread.
    It constantly watches the Redis Queue and processes data in optimized batches.
    """
    print("🚀 ML Worker started. Waiting for transactions from Redis...")
    # Mock ML Model that accepts arrays for fast matrix computing
    def predict_batch(amounts):
        # High amounts flag higher risk scores
        return [0.95 if amt > 50000 else 0.05 for amt in amounts]
    while True:
        # Pull up to 10 items out of the queue at once to batch process them
        batch_items = []
        # Atomically pop elements from the right side of the list
        # If queue is empty, it blocks and waits without cooking your CPU
        first_item = r.brpop(QUEUE_KEY, timeout=2)
        if first_item:
            # brpop returns a tuple: (queue_name, element)
            batch_items.append(json.loads(first_item[1]))
            # Drain up to 9 more items immediately available in the queue buffer
            while len(batch_items) < 10:
                extra_item = r.rpop(QUEUE_KEY)
                if not extra_item:
                    break
                batch_items.append(json.loads(extra_item))
        if batch_items:
            start_time = time.time()
            # Extract features from the batch efficiently
            amounts = [item["amount"] for item in batch_items]
            # Run matrix ML prediction instantly on the whole batch
            predictions = predict_batch(amounts)
            # Match results back and route outputs
            for item, score in zip(batch_items, predictions):
                status = "BLOCK" if score > 0.5 else "ALLOW"
                # Print output to simulate updating a real-time analytics dashboard
                print(f"[ML EVAL] Tx: {item['transaction_id']} | Amount: ₹{item['amount']} | Score: {score} | Action: {status} | Latency: {round((time.time() - item['ingested_at'])*1000, 2)}ms")
            print(f"📦 Batch of {len(batch_items)} processed in {round((time.time() - start_time)*1000, 2)}ms\n")

In a production-ready streaming architecture, ML models do not run inside Kafka, and they rarely run directly inside Redis. [1] 
Instead, your ML models run inside independent Python worker processes (like the run_ml_worker loop from the previous step) that sit between Kafka and Redis.
Here is exactly where the ML models live, along with the one advanced exception where you can run models inside Redis.
1. Why ML Models Do Not Run Inside Kafka
Kafka is purely a distributed data pipeline (a post office). It is built in Java/Scala to move massive volumes of data records from point A to point B with absolute reliability. It does not have a native Python runtime environment to load heavy ML frameworks like Scikit-Learn, PyTorch, or XGBoost. [2, 3, 4, 5] 
2. Where They Actually Run: The Python Worker Layer (Standard Industry Practice)
You run your ML models in dedicated Python scripts or containerized microservices (using Docker) that sit outside both systems. [6] 
The Flow: Kafka streams the transaction data → Redis queues it → Your Python microservice pulls the data from Redis, loads the model into its local RAM using joblib or pickle, runs model.predict(), and pushes the result out. [7, 8] 
Why: This isolates your ML logic. If your ML model runs out of memory or crashes due to a weird data inputs, it will not bring down your Kafka stream or your Redis database.
The Advanced Exception: Running Models Inside Redis (RedisAI)
There is a specialized database module called RedisAI (now part of the Redis Advanced Capabilities). It allows you to load pre-trained deep learning and machine learning models directly into the Redis database infrastructure itself. [9] 
How it works: You export your Python ML model as a .onnx, .pb (TensorFlow), or .pt (PyTorch) file. You upload this file directly into Redis using a command like AI.MODELSET. [10, 11] 
The Benefit: Zero data movement latency. Instead of pulling features out of Redis into Python to run the model, you send the data to Redis, and Redis runs the model instantly inside its own memory space. [12, 13] 
The Catch: It requires installing specialized C-based database extensions and does not natively support standard Python .pkl files.
Which one should you use for your project demo?
For a student or professional project demo, go with the Python Worker Layer. It is significantly easier to build, debug, and present.
Use Kafka to ingest the raw user clicks or transaction bursts.
Use Redis as the high-speed feature store to count the 10-minute transaction windows.
Use a separate Python background script to load your ML model and execute the fraud check. [14, 15, 16]

13. Persistence
Redis is memory-based.
What if server crashes?
Redis offers persistence.
Snapshot (RDB)
Takes periodic snapshots.
RAM
↓
dump.rdb
Fast recovery.
You're thinking about it correctly. RDB snapshots do not guarantee that every write is persisted immediately.
Here's how it works:
Redis stores data in RAM.
Every so often (based on your configuration), it creates a snapshot called dump.rdb.
If the server crashes before the next snapshot, any writes that happened after the last snapshot are lost.
For example:
10:00 AM  → Snapshot created (dump.rdb)
10:01 AM  → User A data written
10:02 AM  → User B data written
10:03 AM  → User C data written
10:04 AM  → Server crashes
When Redis restarts, it restores from the 10:00 AM snapshot.
So the data for Users A, B, and C is gone because it never made it into a snapshot.
Who is responsible for the data loss?
From a technical perspective, this is expected behavior, not a bug.
The responsibility depends on how Redis is configured:
System administrator / DevOps team decides the persistence strategy.
Application architects decide whether some data loss is acceptable.
Redis simply behaves according to the configured settings.
If an application chooses RDB-only persistence, it is accepting the possibility of losing the data written since the last snapshot.
How do people avoid this?
Redis provides another persistence mechanism called AOF (Append Only File).
Instead of taking snapshots periodically, AOF logs every write operation.
SET x 10
SET y 20
DEL z
Depending on the configuration:
appendfsync always → almost no data loss (slowest)
appendfsync everysec → at most about 1 second of data loss (most common)
appendfsync no → OS decides when to flush (more risk, better performance)
Many production deployments use both RDB and AOF:
RDB provides fast startup and compact backups.
AOF minimizes data loss after a crash.
Why would anyone use RDB if it can lose data?
Because it has advantages:
Very fast recovery.
Smaller persistence files.
Lower runtime overhead than logging every write.
Good for use cases where losing the last few minutes of cached or non-critical data is acceptable.
So yes, your observation is correct: RDB snapshots do not guarantee that every record is saved. Any writes made after the last snapshot can be lost if the server crashes. This trade-off is intentional and is one of the reasons Redis offers multiple persistence options so users can choose the balance between performance and durability that fits their application.
AOF (Append Only File)
Every write command recorded.

Doesn't this increase cost?
Yes. More servers mean:
More hardware or cloud instance costs.
More network traffic.
More operational complexity (monitoring, backups, failover, upgrades).
So why do companies still do it?
Because a single server has limits.
Suppose one Redis server has:
64 GB RAM
Can handle 200,000 requests/second
Now imagine your application needs:
500 GB of cached data
2 million requests/second
A single machine simply cannot handle that. No matter how much you optimize, you'll eventually hit hardware limits (RAM, CPU, network bandwidth).
By using a cluster:
The total capacity grows as you add more servers.
Who manages all these servers?
In modern deployments, it's largely automated.
Companies use tools such as:
Kubernetes
Cloud-managed Redis services
Monitoring systems
Automatic failover and replication
So engineers aren't manually moving keys between servers. Redis Cluster automatically decides which server stores a key using hash slots.
Doesn't it become inefficient?
There is some overhead:
Servers communicate over the network, which is slower than memory access within a single machine.
Managing distributed systems is more complex.
However, this overhead is usually much smaller than the benefit of being able to store far more data and handle much higher traffic.
A good rule of thumb is:
If one Redis server is enough, don't use a cluster. It's simpler and cheaper.
If one server is no longer enough because of memory or throughput limits, clustering becomes the practical solution despite the extra cost and complexity.
So clustering is not about making Redis faster than a single server in every situation—it's about scaling beyond what one machine can physically provide.

So Redis stores data in the RAM of the machine where Redis is running, not in your application's memory.
What is RAM?
RAM (Random Access Memory) is the computer's working memory.
Imagine you're studying.
Your setup:
Bookshelf  ← Disk (SSD/HDD)
↓
Take one book
↓
Study Table ← RAM
Your study table is where you're actively working.
You don't keep every book on the table because there's limited space.
RAM is exactly like the study table.
What is Disk?
Disk (SSD/HDD) is permanent storage.
Examples:
Windows
Ubuntu
Games
Photos
Videos
MySQL database files
Everything remains there even after shutting down the computer.
Example:
Disk
Movies
Photos
Chrome
VS Code
Java
PostgreSQL
Turn off the computer.
Turn it on tomorrow.
Everything is still there.
RAM is temporary
Suppose you open Chrome.
Initially:
Disk
Chrome.exe
You double-click Chrome.
The operating system copies Chrome into RAM.
Disk
-------
Chrome.exe
↓
RAM
-------
Chrome Running
CPU executes the instructions from RAM because RAM is much faster than reading directly from disk.
When you close Chrome:
RAM
(empty)
When you shut down the computer:
Everything in RAM disappears.
Why can't programs run directly from disk?
Because disks are much slower.
Approximate access times:
If the CPU had to fetch every instruction from disk, programs would feel extremely slow.
How does retrieval actually work?
Imagine you saved a photo.
photo.jpg
It is stored on the SSD.
When you open it:
CPU asks the operating system for the file.
The operating system reads the file from the SSD.
The file is copied into RAM.
The image viewer reads it from RAM.
The CPU processes it from RAM.
Flow:
SSD
photo.jpg
        │
        ▼
Operating System
        │
        ▼
RAM
photo bytes
        │
        ▼

        │
        ▼
CPU
Great question. The important idea is that RAM is volatile, which means its contents disappear whenever the machine or process can no longer keep that memory alive.
For Redis, data can be lost in several situations.
Case 1: Normal server shutdown (without persistence)
Suppose Redis is running with persistence disabled.
RAM
--------------------
user:1 = Rahul
user:2 = Priya
cart:101 = iPhone
--------------------
You execute:
sudo systemctl stop redis
The Redis process stops.
Its RAM is released back to the operating system.
RAM
--------------------
(empty)
--------------------
When Redis starts again, it begins with an empty database.
Solution:
Enable RDB snapshots
Or AOF
Or both
Case 2: Power failure
Imagine a power outage.
Redis
      ↓
Machine loses electricity
      ↓
RAM loses power
      ↓
Memory becomes empty
Since RAM requires continuous electrical power to retain data, everything not already written to disk is gone.
Solution:
RDB
AOF
UPS (battery backup) to allow graceful shutdown
Case 3: Operating system crash
Example:
Linux Kernel Panic
or
Blue Screen of Death (Windows)
The OS crashes.
Redis is terminated immediately.
RAM contents disappear after reboot.
Any data not persisted is lost.
Solution:
RDB
AOF
Case 4: Redis process crashes
Example:
Redis
↓
Segmentation fault
↓
Process exits
The operating system reclaims the memory used by the Redis process.
If persistence hasn't recorded recent changes, those changes are lost.
Solution:
AOF
Replication (a replica may still have the latest data)
Case 5: Cloud VM crashes
Suppose Redis runs on an AWS EC2 instance.
EC2 Instance
-------------
Redis
64 GB RAM
-------------
The VM crashes because of hardware failure or the instance is terminated.
RAM disappears.
When a replacement VM starts, only persisted data can be restored.
Solution:
Store RDB/AOF on persistent storage (like an EBS volume)
Use Redis replication and automatic failover
Case 6: Accidental restart
Someone runs:
sudo reboot
The machine restarts.
RAM is cleared.
Redis restarts.
If persistence is enabled:
Redis
↓
Reads dump.rdb
or
Reads appendonly.aof
↓
Restores data
Without persistence:
Redis starts empty.
Case 7: Memory eviction (different from RAM loss)
This is not a crash.
Suppose your Redis server has:
RAM = 4 GB
Redis already uses:
3.99 GB
A new key arrives.
There isn't enough memory.
Depending on the configured eviction policy, Redis may automatically remove older or less frequently used keys (for example, using LRU or LFU policies) to make room for the new data.
Old Cache
↓
Deleted
↓
New Cache Inserted
This is intentional behavior, not a failure.
Solution:
Increase available memory.
Configure an appropriate eviction policy.
Use a Redis Cluster to spread data across multiple machines.
Case 8: Last writes not yet persisted
Suppose RDB snapshots occur every 5 minutes.
10:00  Snapshot
10:01  User A
10:02  User B
10:03  User C
10:04  Crash
When Redis restarts:
Loads snapshot from 10:00
Data for Users A, B, and C is lost because it wasn't included in the latest snapshot.
Solution:
Use AOF (appendfsync everysec is a common balance between durability and performance).
Or use both RDB and AOF.
Summary
The key distinction is:
RAM loss happens when the machine or Redis process can no longer retain memory (shutdown, crash, power failure).
Data loss in Redis depends on whether those in-memory changes had already been written to disk through a persistence mechanism like RDB or AOF.
Then why is Redis so fast?
Normally:
Application
↓
Database
↓
Disk
Every query may involve disk access (though databases also use RAM caches internally).
Redis does this instead:
Application
↓
Redis
↓
RAM
No disk read is needed for most operations.
That's why a GET user:10 in Redis can complete in microseconds.
That's an excellent systems-design question. The answer depends on how Redis is deployed.
Scenario 1: Traditional Redis (most common)
Redis is started as a server process and keeps running continuously.
Server
--------------------------
Ubuntu
Redis Process  ✓ Running
--------------------------
Even if nobody sends requests for 3 hours, Redis is still:
occupying RAM
using a tiny amount of CPU
listening for incoming connections
This is intentional because Redis is designed for very low latency (often under 1 ms). If it had to start up on every request, it wouldn't be able to provide that performance.
Isn't that wasting money?
Sometimes, yes.
Imagine an online shopping website.
12 PM - 11 PM
100,000 users
2 AM - 6 AM
50 users
Redis still runs overnight.
You're paying for the server even though it's mostly idle.
But many companies accept this because:
restarting Redis frequently would increase latency,
keeping cached data in memory is valuable,
the cost is justified by the performance benefits.
Does Redis have a cold start like Render?
Not by itself.
Platforms like Render, Vercel, or Railway may put applications to sleep to save infrastructure costs. When the next request arrives, they start the application again, causing a "cold start."
Redis is different:
it is a long-running database server,
it is generally not designed to sleep and wake up on demand.
If you manually stop Redis:
redis-server
↓
Stopped
↓
Next request arrives
↓
Someone has to start Redis again
Redis doesn't automatically wake itself up.
What happens in cloud services?
Managed Redis services (such as those offered by cloud providers) typically keep Redis running 24/7.
Why?
Because databases are expected to be available immediately.
If every query had to wait 20 seconds while Redis started, applications would feel slow and unreliable.
What resources does an idle Redis use?
Suppose:
Redis
100 GB cached data
Even with no traffic:
RAM remains allocated.
CPU usage is usually close to zero.
Network usage is minimal.
The Redis process continues running.
Most of the ongoing cost comes from the memory allocated to the server, not from CPU usage.
How do companies reduce costs?
They use several strategies depending on their workload:
Right-size the instance: Choose a server with only as much RAM as needed.
Scale vertically or horizontally: Increase or decrease resources as demand changes.
Use eviction policies: Cache only the most valuable data instead of everything.
Run Redis only where it provides value: Not every application needs Redis.
For workloads that are truly infrequent, some teams may even choose not to use Redis and instead rely directly on a database.
Can Redis ever be started on demand?
Yes, but it's uncommon.
For example:
Request arrives
↓
Start Redis container
↓
Load persistence file
↓
Accept requests
This introduces startup delay because Redis must:
start the process,
allocate memory,
load the RDB or AOF file into RAM.
For a large dataset, this can take from seconds to minutes, which is why production systems that depend on Redis for low latency generally avoid this pattern.
The key trade-off
Redis is a service optimized for speed, not for minimizing idle infrastructure costs.
Serverless platforms optimize for cost by allowing applications to sleep when idle, accepting occasional cold starts.
Redis optimizes for immediate response times by staying in memory and ready to serve requests, even if that means paying for allocated resources while it's idle.
That's why you'll usually see Redis running continuously in production systems where fast access is more important than eliminating idle cost.
But if RAM loses everything, doesn't Redis lose data?
Yes—unless it saves the data to disk.
Redis periodically writes its in-memory data to disk.
RAM
Alice
Bob
Charlie
↓
Snapshot
↓
dump.rdb (Disk)
Or it logs each write operation to an append-only file.
If the server restarts:
Disk
↓
Redis starts
↓
Loads data back into RAM
This is why Redis supports persistence (RDB snapshots and AOF logs).
Where does the operating system fit in?
Your application never talks directly to RAM or disk.
Everything goes through the operating system.
Application
↓
Operating System
↓
RAM / SSD
The operating system:
Allocates RAM to programs.
Frees RAM when programs exit.
Reads and writes files on disk.
Prevents programs from accessing each other's memory.
How does Redis get RAM?
Suppose a server has 16 GB of RAM.
Initially:
16 GB RAM
Free: 16 GB
You start Redis.
Redis asks the operating system:
"Please give me memory."
The operating system allocates memory to the Redis process.
Example:
16 GB RAM
Redis → 4 GB
Java App → 2 GB
MySQL → 5 GB
Free → 5 GB
Redis now stores all its keys and values in the 4 GB allocated to it.
A complete request example
Suppose a user requests a product page.
Browser

Yes

Product returned
↓

↓

The first request is slower because it reads from the database. Later requests are much faster because they hit Redis in memory.
One more important point
You might wonder: "If databases use disks, why aren't they always slow?"
Modern databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL also keep frequently accessed data in RAM using a buffer cache. The difference is that they are designed for durable, long-term storage and complex queries, while Redis is designed as an in-memory data store where the primary copy of the data lives in RAM. That design lets Redis optimize for extremely fast key-based reads and writes.
Understanding this distinction—disk for persistence, RAM for speed—is the key idea behind why Redis is used alongside traditional databases rather than replacing them.
This is the exact question that makes Redis "click" for most people. The important realization is:
Redis is not caching data for a specific user. It is caching data for the entire application.

The complete picture

The key idea to remember
Redis is not a per-user cache. It's a shared cache for your application.
The backend decides what key to use (for example, product:100, category:electronics, or user:42:profile). Whenever two requests generate the same cache key, they read the same cached data. Whenever they generate different keys, Redis stores separate entries. That's how millions of users can efficiently share cached data without interfering with each other.
This is one of the most important concepts in system design. Think of MongoDB/MySQL and Redis as serving different purposes.
MongoDB/MySQL = Source of Truth (permanent storage)
Redis = Fast temporary storage (cache + ephemeral data)
Let's use an Amazon/Flipkart-like e-commerce website.
What is stored in MySQL/MongoDB?

Redis stores data that needs to be accessed very quickly or doesn't need to be permanent.

Suppose an e-commerce company has:

How long is data kept?

What happens if Redis loses data?

This is called a cache miss.
Redis rebuilds itself from the primary database as users access data.
What if MongoDB loses data?
This is much more serious.
Suppose
Orders
↓
Deleted
You cannot ask customers to place their orders again.
So databases have stronger durability mechanisms.
They typically use:
transaction logs (write-ahead logs or oplogs, depending on the database),
backups,
replication,
point-in-time recovery.
Recovery is done by restoring from backups and replaying logged operations to recover changes made after the backup.
How is data stored?
Redis
Imagine a cluster of 3 servers.
Redis Cluster
Server A
Product Cache
Server B
Session Data

Cart Data
More precisely, Redis uses hashing to distribute keys across servers, and each primary node usually has one or more replicas for failover.

Replica B

MongoDB

MySQL

Final comparison
The mental model
Think of an e-commerce system like a library:
MongoDB/MySQL is the master archive. Every official record is kept there permanently.
Redis is the librarian's desk. It holds the books that people are asking for right now so they can be handed out quickly.
If the librarian's desk is cleared, the books can be fetched again from the archive. If the archive itself is lost, recovering the library becomes a much bigger challenge.

concepts.title: sql indexing related.docx
concepts.content:
When you use an index, the database engine expects to jump straight to a specific location (like looking up a word in a dictionary index). [1, 2, 3] 
However, when you ask a database to find everything not equal to a value, you are forcing it to look for almost the entire dataset. This often causes the optimizer to completely ignore the index and read the entire table from disk line by line. This process is called a Full Table Scan. [4, 5, 6] 
How Indexes Work (The Analogy)
Imagine a physical phone book sorted alphabetically by city.
Equal (=): "Find people living in 'Miami'." You jump straight to the "M" section. The index works perfectly.
Not Equal (<>): "Find people not living in 'Miami'." You cannot jump to one specific section. You now have to read the entire phone book from page one to the end to find every city that isn't Miami. [7] 
Why MySQL Abandons the Index
MySQL uses a cost-based optimizer to decide the fastest way to run your query. [8, 9] 
The Threshold: If MySQL estimates that a query will return more than roughly 20% to 30% of the rows in a table, using an index actually becomes slower than just reading the raw table data. [10] 
The Penalty: Using an index requires two steps: looking up the pointer in the index, then fetching the actual row data from the disk. [11, 12, 13] 
The Decision: Because a NOT EQUAL condition usually matches the vast majority of your data (e.g., 99% of customers do not have a referee ID of 2), MySQL decides it is faster to just scan the whole table from top to bottom rather than jumping back and forth using an index. [14, 15] 
How to Fix It (The Solutions)
If you are dealing with millions of rows and a not-equal query is killing your performance, you can use these workarounds:
1. Flip it to a Positive Condition (Range Scan)
If you are filtering numbers or dates, rewrite the inequality into a range. MySQL handles range indexes (< and >) much better than it handles <>. [16, 17] 
-- Slow (Triggers Full Scan)
SELECT * FROM Customer WHERE referee_id <> 2;
-- Faster (Uses Index Range Scan)
SELECT * FROM Customer WHERE referee_id < 2 OR referee_id > 2;
2. Use a Covering Index
If your index contains all the columns requested in your SELECT statement, MySQL does not have to look at the actual table disk space at all. It can perform a scan entirely inside the much smaller index memory space (Index Scan), which is significantly faster than a Full Table Scan. [18, 19, 20, 21, 22] 
-- If you create this index:
CREATE INDEX idx_referee_name ON Customer(referee_id, name);
-- This query becomes fast because 'name' and 'referee_id' are both in the index:
SELECT name FROM Customer WHERE referee_id <> 2;
If you are trying to speed up a slow query, let me know:
How many rows are currently in your table?
What columns are you selecting, and which ones are in your WHERE clause?
Do you know how to run an EXPLAIN statement to check your query path?

concepts.title: state management.docx
concepts.content:
What is State Management?
In software development, state is the memory of your application [MDN Web Docs Prototypal Inheritance]. It is the data that changes over time based on user interactions, API responses, or system events. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] 
Examples of state include:
Is the user logged in? (Boolean: true / false)
What items are in the shopping cart? (Array of objects)
Is a page currently loading? (Boolean)
What theme is active? (String: "light" or "dark")
State Management is the system and architectural design you use to store, track, and modify this data cleanly across your entire application. Without proper state management, different parts of an app can become "out of sync" (e.g., a navbar showing 0 items in a cart, while the checkout page shows 3 items). [6] 
What External Things Are Used For It?
As applications grow, passing data manually between components becomes a nightmare (a problem called "prop drilling"). To solve this, developers use external tools, libraries, or frameworks to act as a single source of truth. [7, 8] 
The choice of tool depends entirely on the framework and the environment you are working in:
1. In React and Next.js (Client-Side State) [9] 
These tools store state inside the user's browser memory so the UI responds instantly to changes.
Zustand: The current industry favorite. It is ultra-lightweight, fast, uses functional hooks, and requires almost zero boilerplate code. [10, 11] 
Redux Toolkit (RTK): The traditional enterprise standard. It uses a strict, structured architecture (Actions, Reducers, Dispatches) that is excellent for massive, complex apps, though it requires more setup. [12, 13, 14, 15, 16] 
MobX: An object-oriented approach that uses observables to automatically update the UI when data properties change. [17, 18, 19, 20] 
Recoil / Jotai: Atomic state systems where you break your state down into tiny, independent pieces ("atoms") that components can subscribe to. [21, 22, 23, 24] 
2. In Next.js and Modern Web Apps (Server-State Caching)
Instead of syncing UI data, these external libraries focus on syncing data between your frontend UI and your backend database.
TanStack Query (React Query): Handles data fetching, caching, synchronization, and automatic background re-fetching so you don't have to manage API loading/error states manually.
3. In Distributed Backend Systems / AI Agents (Global Backend State) [25, 26, 27] 
When state needs to persist across multiple servers, backend processes, or AI LLM loops, you cannot store it in the browser's memory. You use external infrastructure.
Redis: As discussed earlier, Redis is highly popular for storing backend session state, user tokens, and rate limits because it is fast enough to keep up with server requests.
PostgreSQL / MongoDB: Traditional databases are used when state must be permanently saved (e.g., LangGraph workflow checkpoints, user profiles, order histories). [28, 29] 
Summary Checklist: Choosing a State Tool
Need a simple global variable in a React/Next.js frontend? Use Zustand.
Building a massive React app with strict data tracking? Use Redux Toolkit.
Tired of manually handling API loading and caching states? Use TanStack Query.
Need to share real-time state across multiple servers or API instances? Use Redis. [30, 31, 32, 33]

FRONTEND.title: all hooks.docx
FRONTEND.content:
React Hooks are one of the most important concepts in modern React and Next.js. Since Next.js uses React, the hooks are mostly the same. A good way to understand hooks is: A hook is a special React function that lets a functional component "connect" to React features like state, lifecycle behavior, references, and context. Before hooks, React used class components: class Counter extends React.Component { state = { count: 0 }; render() { return

{this.state.count}

; } } Hooks allow the same thing in a simpler functional style: function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return

{count}

; } 1. useState (Most commonly used) What is useState? useState allows a component to store data that can change over time. Examples: Input values Counters Toggle buttons Modal open/close state Loading states User selections API response data The important point: Changing state causes React to re-render the component. Basic syntax const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue); Example: const [count, setCount] = useState(0); This creates: count Current value: 0 setCount Function used to update it: setCount(5) How useState works internally Example: function Counter(){ const [count,setCount] = useState(0); return ( ); } Initial render: count = 0 Button shows: 0 User clicks button. This runs: setCount(count + 1) which becomes: setCount(1) React says: State changed. I need to render this component again. New render: count = 1 Button shows: 1 Connection of useState: Where does it connect? Think of this: const [name,setName] = useState(""); You have three connections: User Input | | ↓ setName() | | ↓ React State | | ↓ Component Re-render | | ↓ UI updates Example: Form input Suppose you have: function Login(){ const [email,setEmail] = useState(""); return ( setEmail(e.target.value)} /> ); } Let's trace it. Initial: email="" Input: Empty input. User types: john@gmail.com Browser gives: e.target.value which is: "john@gmail.com" Then: setEmail("john@gmail.com") React updates state. New render: email="john@gmail.com" Input becomes: This is called a: controlled component because React controls the input value. useState with objects Example user profile: const [user,setUser] = useState({ name:"", age:0 }); Updating: Wrong: setUser({ name:"John" }); Why? Because you removed age. New state: { name:"John" } Correct: setUser({ ...user, name:"John" }); Spread keeps existing values: { name:"John", age:0 } useState with arrays Example: const [todos,setTodos] = useState([]); Adding: setTodos([ ...todos, newTodo ]); Example: Before: [ "Study" ] After: [ "Study", "Code" ] When to use useState? Use it when: ✅ UI changes based on data Examples: isModalOpen isLoading username searchText selectedItem cartItems Do NOT use it for: values that don't affect UI temporary calculations 2. useEffect What is useEffect? useEffect runs code after rendering. Used for: API calls subscriptions timers updating external systems Think: "After React displays this component, do this extra work." Syntax: useEffect(() => { }, []); Example: Fetch data function Users(){ const [users,setUsers]=useState([]); useEffect(()=>{ fetch("/api/users") .then(res=>res.json()) .then(data=>setUsers(data)); },[]); return ( <> {users.map(user=>

{user.name}

)} ) } Flow: Component loads: Render | | ↓ useEffect runs | | ↓ API call | | ↓ setUsers() | | ↓ Re-render Why empty array []? useEffect(()=>{ fetchData(); },[]); Means: "Run only once when component mounts." Like: Page opened | ↓ Fetch data Dependency array Example: useEffect(()=>{ console.log(search); },[search]); Means: Run whenever search changes. Example: User types: react Effect runs. Types: react hooks Effect runs again. Cleanup Example timer: useEffect(()=>{ const timer=setInterval(()=>{ console.log("running"); },1000); return ()=>{ clearInterval(timer); } },[]); Why cleanup? Because otherwise every time component loads, a new timer starts. When to use useEffect? Use when something happens outside React: ✅ API calls ✅ timers ✅ browser events ✅ subscriptions Do not use it for: ❌ simple calculations Example: Wrong: useEffect(()=>{ setTotal(price*quantity) },[price,quantity]) Better: const total=price*quantity; 3. useRef What is useRef? useRef stores a value that: survives re-renders does NOT cause re-render when changed Syntax: const ref = useRef(initialValue); Example: Access input directly function Search(){ const inputRef=useRef(); function focusInput(){ inputRef.current.focus(); } return( <> ) } Connection: useRef | | ↓ DOM element | | ↓ inputRef.current Difference: useState: change value | ↓ re-render useRef: change value | ↓ no re-render Use cases: focus input store previous value timers DOM manipulation 4. useContext Problem: Passing props deeply: App | Navbar | UserMenu | Avatar You need user data everywhere. Without context: This is called: prop drilling useContext solves this. Create context: const UserContext=createContext(); Provider: Anywhere: const user=useContext(UserContext); Now component gets user directly. Use for: logged-in user theme language settings 5. useMemo What is useMemo? Caches expensive calculations. Example: const result = useMemo(()=>{ return expensiveFunction(data); },[data]); Without useMemo: Every render: calculate again With useMemo: data unchanged? | ↓ use old result Example: const total = useMemo(()=>{ return products.reduce( (sum,p)=>sum+p.price,0 ) },[products]); Use when: expensive calculations large lists performance optimization Do not use everywhere. 6. useCallback Similar to useMemo, but for functions. Problem: Every render creates a new function: function handleClick(){ } useCallback remembers it. Example: const handleClick=useCallback(()=>{ console.log("clicked"); },[]); Useful when passing functions to child components. Real Next.js Example Combining Hooks A job page: function JobPage(){ const [job,setJob]=useState(null); const [loading,setLoading]=useState(true); useEffect(()=>{ fetch("/api/job") .then(res=>res.json()) .then(data=>{ setJob(data); setLoading(false); }) },[]); if(loading) return

Loading...

return (

{job.title}

) } Here: useState stores: job data loading status useEffect fetches: API data after page loads Most Used Hooks Ranking In real React/Next.js projects: A simple rule: Need changing UI data? → useState Need something after rendering? → useEffect Need to remember something without re-render? → useRef Need global shared data? → useContext Need performance optimization? → useMemo/useCallback In a typical Next.js application, useState + useEffect will be the two hooks you use most frequently.

controlled vs uncontrolled components.docx
FRONTEND.content:
Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components This concept is about who controls the value of an input field. Whenever you have a form like: Login form Signup form Search box Contact form React needs to know where the input value is stored. There are two approaches: Controlled Component → React controls the input. Uncontrolled Component → The browser (DOM) controls the input. 1. Controlled Components A controlled component is an input whose value is controlled by React state. The flow is: User types │ ▼ onChange event │ ▼ setState() │ ▼ React State Updates │ ▼ Component Re-renders │ ▼ Updated value shown in input Notice: The input gets its value from React, not directly from the browser. Example import { useState } from "react"; function Login() { const [email, setEmail] = useState(""); return ( setEmail(e.target.value)} /> ); } Step-by-Step Working Initially: const [email, setEmail] = useState(""); React state: email = "" Input becomes: Empty box. User types: j Browser fires: onChange Inside: setEmail(e.target.value); becomes setEmail("j"); React updates state: email = "j" Component re-renders. Now: User types: jo Again: setEmail("jo"); React updates. Input: Every key press follows this cycle: User ↓ onChange ↓ setState ↓ React State ↓ Re-render ↓ Updated Input This is why it's called Controlled. React is always in control. Why Use Controlled Components? Suppose you want validation. Example: Only allow 10 characters. { if (e.target.value.length <= 10) { setUsername(e.target.value); } }} /> Now React decides what is allowed. Suppose you want: Disable submit button Live search Show character count Password strength Validation All become easy. Example:

Characters: {username.length}

Since React already has the value, it can use it anywhere. Real Login Example function Login() { const [email, setEmail] = useState(""); const [password, setPassword] = useState(""); function handleSubmit(e) { e.preventDefault(); console.log(email); console.log(password); } return (
setEmail(e.target.value)} /> setPassword(e.target.value)} />
); } Notice: When Submit is clicked, React already knows: Email Password because they're stored in state. 2. Uncontrolled Components Here React does not store the input value. Instead, the browser keeps it. React reads it only when needed. Usually with: useRef() Example import { useRef } from "react"; function Login() { const inputRef = useRef(); function handleSubmit() { console.log(inputRef.current.value); } return ( <> ); } Step-by-Step Working Initially: Input empty User types: john@gmail.com Where is it stored? Not in React. It stays inside the HTML input element. Like: React doesn't know or care while the user is typing. Only when: handleSubmit() runs, React asks: inputRef.current.value Browser replies: john@gmail.com Flow: User types ↓ DOM stores value ↓ React does nothing ↓ Submit clicked ↓ Read value using ref Side-by-Side Comparison Controlled const [name, setName] = useState(""); setName(e.target.value)} /> Storage: React State Uncontrolled const inputRef = useRef(); Storage: Browser DOM Controlled vs Uncontrolled Flow Controlled User ↓ Input ↓ onChange ↓ React State ↓ UI Uncontrolled User ↓ Input ↓ DOM stores value ↓ Read using ref Validation Example Suppose password must be 8 characters. Controlled: if(password.length<8){ show error } Easy. Uncontrolled: You don't know the password until: inputRef.current.value is read. Validation happens later. Live Search Example Controlled: setSearch(e.target.value)} /> Every key updates React. You can immediately call: searchProducts(search); Uncontrolled: React doesn't know what user typed. Not suitable for live search. Which One Does React Recommend? Almost always: Controlled Components because: Validation Better debugging Easier state management Easy API integration Predictable behavior Most production React apps use controlled inputs. When Should You Use Uncontrolled Components? Examples: File Upload File inputs are typically handled using refs because browsers restrict setting their value programmatically. Simple Form One input. No validation. Only need value once. Using useRef is acceptable. Third-Party Libraries Some libraries manipulate DOM directly. Then refs become useful. Interview Question Which is better? Generally: Controlled Components because React knows everything happening inside the form. Advantages of Controlled Components ✅ Easy validation ✅ Instant UI updates ✅ Better debugging ✅ Form reset is easy setEmail(""); Input clears automatically. Advantages of Uncontrolled Components ✅ Less code ✅ Slightly fewer React state updates ✅ Good for simple forms Example: Resetting Form Controlled: setEmail(""); Input becomes empty immediately because its value comes from state. Uncontrolled: inputRef.current.value = ""; You have to modify the DOM element directly. Summary Simple way to remember Controlled Component → React controls the input. Uncontrolled Component → The browser controls the input, and React reads it later. const inputRef = useRef();

Git.content:
• 
Git is not the same as GitHub. 
• 
GitHub makes tools that use Git. 
• 
GitHub is the largest host of source code in the world, and has 
been owned by Microsoft since 2018. 
• 
Over 70% of developers use Git! 
• 
Developers can work together from anywhere in the world. 
• 
Developers can see the full history of the project. 
• 
Developers can revert to earlier versions of a project. 
 
What is Git :- 
Why Git :- 
What is GitHub :- 
Features of Git :- 
• 
When a file is changed, added or deleted, it is considered 
modified 
• 
You select the modified files you want to Stage 
• 
The Staged files are Committed, which prompts Git to store a 
permanent snapshot of the files 
• 
Git allows you to see the full history of every commit. 
• 
You can revert back to any previous commit. 
• 
Git does not store a separate copy of every file in every 
commit, but keeps track of changes made in each commit! 
• Git is a version control system. 
• Git helps you keep track of code changes. 
• Git is used to collaborate on code. 
• Git and GitHub are different things. 


![PDF Image Page 1](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514156/revision_notes/hfutyjrikdcgnogmzbgy.png)



![PDF Image Page 1](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514156/revision_notes/fidtfcn6z5n23dbdps3m.png)

 
 
 
 
 
$ git config --global user.name “<Enter your username here>” 
$ git config --global user.email “<Enter your email here>” 
Configuring git for the first time :- 
Initializing Git :- 
Git now knows that it should watch the folder you initiated it 
on. Git creates a hidden folder to keep track of changes. 
$ git init 
Staging files/Adding files to Git repo :- 
$ git add <filename with extension> 
Staging all files in a folder :- 
$ git add --all 
$ git add -A 
OR 
Staged files are files that are ready to be committed to the 
repository you are working on. 
When you first add files to an empty repository, they are all 
untracked. To get Git to track them, you need to stage them, or add 
them to the staging environment. 
General Git Features :- 


![PDF Image Page 2](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514157/revision_notes/tom11nmnajxzbdvbqmpz.png)



![PDF Image Page 2](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514158/revision_notes/gua5llrlxosjyfww9gap.png)

![PDF Image Page 2](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514159/revision_notes/qyke2udmgnfmyewaxnjp.png)

 
 
 
Making a Commit :- 
Adding commits keep track of our progress and changes as we 
work. Git considers each commit change point or "save point". It is a 
point in the project you can go back to if you find a bug, or want to 
make a change. 
When we commit, we should always include a message. 
$ git commit -m “<Enter your message here>” 
Git Commit without Stage :- 
Sometimes, when you make small changes, using the staging 
environment seems like a waste of time. It is possible to commit 
changes directly, skipping the staging environment. 
$ git commit -a -m “<Enter your message here>” 
Status of files and log :- 
$ git status 
File status in a more compact way :- 
$ git status --short 
Log of a file :- 
 
Log is used to view the history of commits for a repo. 
$ git log 
$ git log --oneline 


![PDF Image Page 3](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514160/revision_notes/qeb04n7ibzf5vbteg30k.png)



![PDF Image Page 3](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514161/revision_notes/sduewixgal4ltmipv9i4.png)



![PDF Image Page 3](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514162/revision_notes/pfwyym8lwr2os9kowbj8.png)

 
 
 
Git Help :- 
If you are having trouble remembering commands or options 
for commands, you can use Git help. 
$ git <command> -help 
See all the available options for the specific command - 
See all possible commands - 
$ git help --all 
If you find yourself stuck in the list view, SHIFT + G to jump the 
end of the list, then q to exit the view. 
Git Branching :- 
In Git, a branch is a new/separate version of the main repository. 
Branches allow you to work on different parts of a project without 
impacting the main branch. When the work is complete, a branch can be 
merged with the main project.  
We can even switch between branches and work on different 
projects without them interfering with each other. 
 
Making a new Git Branch :- 
$ git branch <name of branch> 
Checking all available Branches :- 
$ git branch 


![PDF Image Page 4](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514162/revision_notes/smhibk9kareqrptayton.png)

![PDF Image Page 4](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514164/revision_notes/rvotf3k0h74eculnboc9.png)

 
 
 
Switching to other Branches :- 
$ git checkout <branch name> 
Making a new branch and directly switching to 
it :- 
$ git checkout -b <branch name> 
Deleting a Branch :- 
$ git branch -d <branch name> 
Merging two Branches :- 
$ git merge <branch name> 
It’s preferred to change/switch to master branch before any branch 
needs to be merged with it. 
This will merge the specified branch with our master branch.

![PDF Image Page 5](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514166/revision_notes/fqwxd5pka50ioa0jqyye.png)

 
 
 
+ 
Working with Github :- 
Create a github account to create your remote repositories. Now, 
create a new repo where we will be uploading our files from local repo. 
 
Note -  Local repository (repo.) means the repo. which is on our system    
whereas, remote repo. means the one which is on other remote system/server, 
for eg. - GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, etc. 


![PDF Image Page 6](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514166/revision_notes/ii2qtqsyb7c45ueulkbm.png)



![PDF Image Page 6](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514167/revision_notes/pgos5o5bqmmvq5211ou7.png)

![PDF Image Page 6](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514169/revision_notes/qkvrqomdjm0gvxc13kf7.png)

 
 
 
+ 
Push local repo to GitHub :- 
Copy the url or the link of the repo that we just created. As an 
example, it should look like this -  https://github.com/durgeshm01722 
/example.git 
Paste the copied url in the below git command. 
$ git remote add origin <paste copied URL here> 
‘git remote add origin <URL>’ specifies that we are adding a remote 
repository, with the specified URL, as an origin to our local Git repo. 
 
Finally, pushing our master branch to the origin URL (remote repo) 
and set it as the default remote branch. 
 
$ git push --set-upstream origin master 
Go back into GitHub and see that the repository has been updated. 
Pushing local repo to github after doing the above 
process at least once :- 
First commit all the changes. Then push all the changes to our 
remote origin i.e. remote repo on github. 
$ git push origin 
Pull local repo from GitHub :- 
Git pull is used to pull all changes from a remote repository into the 
branch we are working on. It is a combination of fetch and merge. Use it 
to update your local Git. 
 
$ git pull origin 


![PDF Image Page 7](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514169/revision_notes/hoazfifqdoebekun0kkx.png)

+ 
Pull branch from GitHub :- 
First, check which branches we have and where are we working at 
the moment by ‘git branch’ command. Since we do not have the new 
branch on out local Git which is to be pulled from the Github. So, to see all 
local and remote branches, use - 
$ git branch -a 
For viewing only remote branches :- 
$ git branch -r 
Now, the new branch is seen in the console but it is not available on 
our local repo. So, let’s check it out using ‘git checkout <branch name>’. 
Now run ‘git pull’ to pull that branch on our local repo. We can now check 
the available branches using ‘git branch’. 
Push branch to GitHub :- 
First, let’s create a new local branch which we will be pushing to 
Github. Enter the command as ‘git checkout -b <branch name>’. You can 
check the status of the files in this current branch using ‘git status’. 
Commit all the uncommitted changes for all the files in this branch using 
‘git commit -a -m “<Message>” ’. Now push this branch from our local 
repo to Github using ‘git push origin <branch name>’. 
Git clone from GitHub :- 
We can clone a forked repo from Github on our local repo. A clone is 
a full copy of a repository, including all logging and versions of files. Move 
back to the original repository, and click the green "Code" button to get 
the URL to clone. Copy the URL.

+ 
Now in the git bash, enter the following command to clone the 
copied repo onto your local machine -  
$ git clone <copied URL> 
To specify a specific folder to clone to, add the name of the folder 
after the repository URL, like this - 
$ git clone <copied URL> <folder name>

Git Undo :- 
Git Revert :- 
‘revert’ is the command we use when we want to take a previous 
commit and add it as a new commit, keeping the log intact. First thing, we 
need to find the point we want to return to. To do that, we need to go 
through the log. To avoid the very long log list, use the --oneline option 
which gives just one line per commit showing –  
i. The first seven characters of the commit hash 
ii. The commit message 
Git Revert HEAD :- 
We revert the latest commit using ‘git revert HEAD’ (revert the latest 
change, and then commit). By adding the option --no-edit, we can skip the 
commit message editor (getting the default revert message). 
$ git revert HEAD --no-edit 
Git Revert to any commit :- 
To revert to earlier commits, use ‘git revert HEAD~x’ (x being a 
number. 1 going back one more, 2 going back two more, etc.) 
Git Reset :- 
‘reset’ is the command we use when we want to move the repository 
back to a previous commit, discarding any changes made after that commit. 
First, get the seven characters of the commit hash from the log for the 
commit that you want to go back for. Then we reset our repository back to 
that specific commit using ‘git reset commithash’ (commithash being the first 
7 characters of the commit hash we found in the log). 


![PDF Image Page 10](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514181/revision_notes/wxwlokf0zxbhbqgelb87.png)



![PDF Image Page 10](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514182/revision_notes/kh0sxemj9rxbwr3uacpp.png)



![PDF Image Page 10](https://res.cloudinary.com/dmcfv5gxi/image/upload/v1787514182/revision_notes/azkdwjlkbzmushovp6as.png)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
$ git reset <commithash> 
Git Undo Reset :- 
Even though the commits are no longer showing up in the log, it is not 
removed from Git. If we know the commit hash, we can reset to it using ‘git 
reset <commithash>’. 
Git Amend :- 
commit --amend is used to modify the most recent commit. It combines 
changes in the staging environment with the latest commit, and creates a 
new commit. This new commit replaces the latest commit entirely. 
One of the simplest things you can do with --amend is to change a 
commit message. 
$ git commit --amend -m “<Commit Message>” 
Using this, the previous commit is replaced with our amended one. 
Git Amend Files :- 
Adding files with --amend works the same way as above. Just add them 
to the staging environment before committing.
