short concept all stacks.content:
Yes — if you mean a plain React frontend, not Next.js, then you're probably remembering a structure commonly used with React Router. As of August 2026, React itself does not prescribe a pages/ folder structure. React is the UI library; routing and project structure are separate choices. A common production React structure is: frontend/ ├── src/ │ ├── pages/ │ │ ├── Dashboard/ │ │ │ ├── Dashboard.jsx │ │ │ └── Dashboard.css │ │ │ │ │ ├── Login/ │ │ │ └── Login.jsx │ │ │ │ │ └── Alerts/ │ │ └── Alerts.jsx │ │ │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── Navbar/ │ │ │ └── Navbar.jsx │ │ ├── Sidebar/ │ │ │ └── Sidebar.jsx │ │ └── Button/ │ │ └── Button.jsx │ │ │ ├── hooks/ │ │ ├── useAlerts.js │ │ └── useDashboard.js │ │ │ ├── services/ │ │ └── api.js │ │ │ ├── context/ │ │ └── AuthContext.jsx │ │ │ ├── utils/ │ │ └── formatDate.js │ │ │ ├── App.jsx │ └── main.jsx │ ├── public/ ├── package.json └── vite.config.js But you're remembering something slightly different You may be thinking of: pages/ ├── Dashboard/ │ └── index.jsx ├── Login/ │ └── index.jsx └── Alerts/ └── index.jsx or: pages/ ├── Dashboard.jsx ├── Login.jsx └── Alerts.jsx Both patterns have been common. The important thing is that React doesn't automatically treat pages/Dashboard/page.jsx as a route. That's where the difference from Next.js matters. React + React Router With a modern React application, you'd commonly use React Router for routing. Your structure could be: src/ ├── pages/ │ ├── Dashboard/ │ │ └── Dashboard.jsx │ ├── Login/ │ │ └── Login.jsx │ └── Alerts/ │ └── Alerts.jsx │ ├── components/ ├── hooks/ ├── services/ ├── App.jsx └── main.jsx Then your routes are explicitly defined: const router = createBrowserRouter([ { path: "/", element: , }, { path: "/login", element: , }, { path: "/alerts", element: , }, ]); So: URL React component / → Dashboard.jsx /login → Login.jsx /alerts → Alerts.jsx This is different from Next.js In Next.js: app/ ├── dashboard/ │ └── page.jsx ├── login/ │ └── page.jsx └── alerts/ └── page.jsx The folder structure creates the routes. In normal React: pages/ ├── Dashboard/ │ └── Dashboard.jsx ├── Login/ │ └── Login.jsx └── Alerts/ └── Alerts.jsx The folders are just organization. React Router defines the routes. For your React + FastAPI project I'd recommend something like this rather than copying a Next.js structure: project/ │ ├── frontend/ │ ├── src/ │ │ │ │ │ ├── pages/ │ │ │ ├── Dashboard/ │ │ │ │ └── Dashboard.jsx │ │ │ ├── Analytics/ │ │ │ │ └── Analytics.jsx │ │ │ ├── Alerts/ │ │ │ │ └── Alerts.jsx │ │ │ ├── Chat/ │ │ │ │ └── Chat.jsx │ │ │ └── Login/ │ │ │ └── Login.jsx │ │ │ │ │ ├── components/ │ │ │ ├── Navbar/ │ │ │ ├── Sidebar/ │ │ │ ├── DataTable/ │ │ │ ├── KPICard/ │ │ │ └── Chart/ │ │ │ │ │ ├── hooks/ │ │ │ ├── useAlerts.js │ │ │ ├── useAnalytics.js │ │ │ └── useChat.js │ │ │ │ │ ├── services/ │ │ │ ├── api.js │ │ │ ├── alerts.js │ │ │ ├── analytics.js │ │ │ └── chat.js │ │ │ │ │ ├── context/ │ │ │ └── AuthContext.jsx │ │ │ │ │ ├── utils/ │ │ ├── types/ │ │ ├── App.jsx │ │ └── main.jsx │ │ │ ├── public/ │ ├── package.json │ └── vite.config.js │ └── backend/ ├── app/ │ ├── api/ │ ├── services/ │ ├── models/ │ ├── schemas/ │ ├── repositories/ │ └── main.py │ └── tests/ So if you're asking "Was it pages → folder → page.jsx?", that's primarily the Next.js App Router convention: app/ └── dashboard/ └── page.jsx For plain React, you can absolutely have: pages/ └── Dashboard/ └── Dashboard.jsx but page.jsx has no special meaning to React itself. It's simply a filename you chose. Yes. If you want to understand React properly, it's useful to go one level below components and hooks and understand what actually happens when React runs your application. I'll explain it from browser → React → component → hooks → DOM, and then the important internal concepts. 1. First: React itself doesn't run your application This is an important distinction. When you create a React app, you have something like: Browser ↓ JavaScript ↓ React ↓ Your Components ↓ DOM React is a JavaScript library. The browser actually executes JavaScript. For a modern React project, you might use Vite to develop/build the application. So roughly: Browser ↓ Loads index.html ↓ Loads JavaScript bundle ↓ JavaScript executes ↓ React starts ↓ React renders your App 2. main.jsx is usually where React starts A typical React application has: import React from "react"; import ReactDOM from "react-dom/client"; import App from "./App"; ReactDOM.createRoot( document.getElementById("root") ).render( ); This is essentially saying: "React, take my App component and render it inside the HTML element called root." Your HTML might contain:
So initially: HTML
React takes control of that area. 3. What is really? This: looks like HTML, but it isn't HTML. It's JSX. Conceptually, JSX gets transformed into JavaScript representing a React element. For example: is conceptually similar to: React.createElement(App) Modern React tooling may use the newer JSX transform, so you don't necessarily write React.createElement yourself. The important idea is: JSX is JavaScript syntax that describes what UI you want. 4. React doesn't immediately create DOM for every JSX element This is one of the most important concepts. Suppose you write: function App() { return (

Hello

); } You might imagine React immediately doing: Create div Create h1 Create text Create button Put everything into browser DOM But React first creates an internal representation of the UI. This is where the React Fiber architecture comes in. 5. React Fiber Modern React uses an internal architecture called Fiber. You don't normally interact with Fiber directly. Think of Fiber as React's internal system for representing and processing your component tree. Your application: App ├── Navbar ├── Dashboard │ ├── KPICard │ ├── Chart │ └── Table └── Footer React internally maintains information corresponding to this tree. Very roughly: Fiber tree App │ ├── Navbar ├── Dashboard │ ├── KPICard │ ├── Chart │ └── Table └── Footer A Fiber node contains information React needs to manage that part of the application. Among other things, React tracks things such as: component type props state relationships to other components pending work effects DOM association where applicable You generally don't manipulate Fiber yourself. 6. React has a rendering phase Suppose you have: function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return

{count}

; } Initially: count = 0 React calls your component: Counter() Your component returns:

0

React determines what the UI should look like. This is the render phase. Think: Render phase = React figures out what the UI should be. 7. Then React commits the changes After React determines what needs to change, it applies the necessary changes to the actual browser DOM. This is the commit phase. So you can think: Render phase ↓ "What should the UI look like?" ↓ React figures out changes ↓ Commit phase ↓ "Apply those changes to the DOM" This distinction is extremely important. 8. What happens when state changes? Let's use: const [count, setCount] = useState(0); The user clicks: Suppose count = 0. User clicks. setCount(1) React receives the state update. Then roughly: State update ↓ React schedules work ↓ Component renders again ↓ React compares the result ↓ React determines necessary changes ↓ Commit ↓ Browser DOM updated The important thing: React does not normally throw away the entire page and recreate everything from scratch. It figures out what needs to change. 9. Reconciliation This comparison process is generally referred to as reconciliation. Suppose the previous UI was:

0

and the new render produces:

1

React can determine: Same

Different text ↓ Update text from 0 → 1 It doesn't need to recreate the entire application. 10. The Virtual DOM You've probably heard: "React uses the Virtual DOM." That's a useful beginner explanation, but it can be misleading if taken too literally. React works with React elements and its Fiber tree, and uses reconciliation to determine changes to the host environment, such as the browser DOM. People commonly call the JavaScript representation of UI the Virtual DOM. Conceptually: Your JSX ↓ React elements ↓ Fiber/reconciliation ↓ Browser DOM changes So don't think: "There is one magical second DOM." Think: "React maintains an internal representation of the UI and uses it to determine what should change in the real DOM." 11. What is the real DOM? The browser has an actual DOM:

Hello

This is browser-managed. React eventually updates this actual DOM. React isn't the browser. The browser is responsible for: parsing HTML executing JavaScript layout painting events displaying pixels React helps manage the UI state and updates. 12. Where do components fit? Consider: function App() { return ; } Then: function Dashboard() { return ( <> ); } React builds a component tree: App │ └── Dashboard ├── Navbar ├── Chart └── Table React uses this structure to determine what needs to render and update. 13. Components are just functions — mostly A functional component: function Dashboard() { return

Dashboard

; } is a JavaScript function. React calls it. Conceptually: React ↓ Dashboard() ↓ JSX result ↓ React processes result But React adds a lot of machinery around component execution: state hooks scheduling reconciliation effects context refs rendering priorities That's what makes it much more than simply calling functions manually. 14. How does useState actually work internally? You write: const [count, setCount] = useState(0); React internally associates that state with the component's Fiber/hook data. Conceptually: Counter Fiber │ └── Hooks │ ├── State: 0 └── Update information When: setCount(1); is called, React schedules a state update. Then React renders the component again. Before: count = 0 ↓ setCount(1) After: count = 1 React knows which component and hook the update belongs to. 15. Why must hooks be called in the same order? This is why you cannot do: if (loggedIn) { useState(...); } or: for (...) { useState(...); } React relies on the order of hooks to associate hook calls with their stored state. Imagine: function App() { const [name, setName] = useState(""); const [age, setAge] = useState(0); } React can conceptually think: Hook #1 → name Hook #2 → age If you conditionally change the order: Render 1: Hook #1 → name Hook #2 → age Render 2: Hook #1 → age Hook #2 → name React's association would break. That's the deeper reason behind the Rules of Hooks. 16. What happens with useEffect? Consider: useEffect(() => { fetchData(); }, []); React doesn't execute the effect during the normal rendering calculation. Instead, React records that an effect needs to be processed. Conceptually: Render ↓ React sees useEffect ↓ Records effect ↓ Commit UI ↓ Effect runs That's why useEffect is for side effects, not for calculating what the UI should look like. 17. Why shouldn't you fetch data directly during rendering? Avoid: function Dashboard() { fetch("/api/data"); // ❌ return
Dashboard
; } Why? Because React may render your component more than once. Rendering should ideally be pure. Instead, side effects are separated: useEffect(() => { fetch("/api/data"); }, []); 18. What does "pure rendering" mean? Ideally: function Price({ price }) { return

{price}

; } Given: price = 100 you should get the same UI:

100

Rendering should primarily answer: "Given these props and state, what should the UI look like?" Not: "Send an email, modify the database, start a timer, change some random global variable..." Those are side effects. 19. React's scheduler This is another important internal concept. React doesn't necessarily treat every piece of work as equally urgent. For example: User typing is highly interactive. While: Rendering a large update may be less urgent. Modern React has a scheduling system that allows React to manage rendering work and priorities. This is particularly important with React's concurrent rendering capabilities. You don't manually control Fiber scheduling in normal application code. Think: React decides when and how to process rendering work so the UI remains responsive. 20. Concurrent rendering This does not mean: "React renders everything simultaneously." Instead, React can work on rendering without necessarily blocking everything, and can pause, continue, restart, or abandon rendering work before committing it. Conceptually: Large rendering task ↓ React starts work ↓ Higher-priority interaction arrives ↓ React can prioritize that work ↓ Continue/redo lower-priority work This is one of the major differences between modern React and older mental models of React. 21. short concept all stacks.title: render re-render update.docx
short concept all stacks.content:
Yes. These terms are confusing at first because people often use render, re-render, update, and DOM update as if they mean the same thing. They don't. For React, the most useful mental model is: State/props change ↓ Re-render ↓ React figures out what changed ↓ DOM update ↓ Browser paints the change Let's break each term down. 1. What is "render"? In React, rendering means React runs your component to figure out what the UI should look like. Example: function App() { return

Hello

; } React runs: App() ↓

Hello

So you can think: Render = React calculates/describes the UI. It does not necessarily mean pixels are immediately drawn on the screen. 2. What is the DOM? DOM = Document Object Model. It's the browser's representation of your HTML page. If your page is:

Hello

the browser creates a DOM structure roughly like: Document └── body ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" └── button └── "Click" React eventually updates this DOM. 3. Initial render When your application starts: createRoot(document.getElementById("root")) .render(); React performs the initial render. Conceptually: App() ↓ JSX ↓ React processes it ↓ DOM created/updated ↓ Browser displays it For example: function App() { return

Hello

; } The browser ends up displaying: Hello 4. What is a re-render? A re-render means React runs the component again to determine what the UI should look like now. Example: function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( ); } Initially: count = 0 UI: 0 User clicks. setCount(1) React schedules an update. Then: Counter() runs again ↓ count = 1 ↓ React gets That's a re-render. 5. Does re-render mean the whole webpage gets recreated? No. This is a very common misconception. Suppose your page contains: Navbar Dashboard Chart Table Footer You change the number in one KPI card. React may re-render components, but it doesn't simply destroy the entire browser page and rebuild every DOM element. React compares the new result with the previous result and determines what needs to change. Conceptually: Before:

100

After:

101

React realizes: Same h1 Different text ↓ Update text 100 → 101 6. Render ≠ DOM update This distinction is very important. Suppose: const [count, setCount] = useState(0); You call: setCount(1); React will generally: 1. Schedule an update 2. Re-render the component 3. Compare old/new UI 4. Commit necessary DOM changes So: RENDER = Figure out what UI should look like DOM UPDATE = Actually change the browser's DOM 7. What is "reconciliation"? You've heard this term too. Reconciliation is React's process of figuring out how the new UI relates to the previous UI. For example: Previous:

Hello

100 users

New:

Hello

101 users

React determines:
→ same

→ same "Hello" → same

→ same "100 users" → "101 users" Therefore only the necessary part needs updating. You can think: Reconciliation = React figuring out what changed between renders. 8. What is "commit"? After React determines what needs to change, it applies those changes. That's the commit phase. Simplified: Render ↓ "What should the UI look like?" ↓ Reconciliation ↓ "What changed?" ↓ Commit ↓ "Apply those changes to DOM" 9. What is "paint"? Now we're getting closer to the browser itself. After the DOM and styles have been updated, the browser needs to actually display pixels. Very simplified: React ↓ DOM changes ↓ Browser calculates layout ↓ Browser paints pixels ↓ You see the result So paint is primarily a browser rendering concept, not a React concept. 10. What is "mount"? You'll hear: "When the component mounts..." Mount = the component is being added to the UI for the first time. For example: Login page ↓ User logs in ↓ Dashboard component appears The Dashboard mounted. Think: Mount = component enters the UI. 11. What is "unmount"? The opposite. Unmount = component is removed from the UI. Example: Dashboard ↓ User logs out ↓ Login page The Dashboard is unmounted. This is important for cleanup. For example: useEffect(() => { window.addEventListener("scroll", handleScroll); return () => { window.removeEventListener("scroll", handleScroll); }; }, []); The cleanup runs when the component is unmounted. 12. What is "update"? Update is a broad term. Something changes: state props context etc. React may then perform another render. For example: setPrice(200); causes a state update. That can lead to: State update ↓ Re-render ↓ Reconciliation ↓ DOM update 13. Props changing A component can re-render because its props change. Parent: Suppose: price = 100 Then: price = 200 The parent renders with: The child receives new props. Conceptually: Parent changes ↓ New props ↓ Child may re-render 14. State change vs re-render These are related but aren't the same thing. When you do: setCount(1); you're saying: "I want to update state." React then schedules a render. So: setCount() ↓ state update ↓ React schedules render ↓ component renders again 15. What causes a React component to re-render? The main things you should know are: State update setCount(10); Parent renders A parent rendering can cause its children to render again under normal React behavior, subject to React's optimizations/memoization. Context value changes If a component consumes context and the relevant context value changes, it can re-render. External subscriptions Libraries can trigger updates when subscribed data changes. 16. What does NOT necessarily mean a re-render? Changing a ref: myRef.current = 100; doesn't itself cause a React render. That's one reason useRef is useful. Compare: setCount(100); → React state update → render scheduled. versus: countRef.current = 100; → ref changed → no React render caused by that change. 17. What does useMemo have to do with rendering? Suppose: const result = useMemo(() => { expensiveCalculation(data); }, [data]); Your component can still re-render. useMemo doesn't stop the component from rendering. It can stop the expensive calculation from running again when dependencies haven't changed. That's an important distinction. Component re-renders ↓ useMemo checks dependencies ↓ Data hasn't changed ↓ Reuse previous calculation 18. What does React.memo do? This is another term you'll encounter. const MyComponent = React.memo(Component); It can allow React to skip rendering a component when its props haven't changed, subject to React's behavior and the component's context/state. So: Normal component: Parent renders ↓ Child may render again Memoized component: Parent renders ↓ Props unchanged? ↓ Potentially skip child render This is a performance optimization. Don't automatically wrap every component in React.memo. 19. Render vs re-render The easiest distinction: Render The component is being rendered. Component → UI description Re-render The component has already rendered and React renders it again because something changed/another update occurred. First render ↓ State/props/context/etc. update ↓ Re-render 20. A complete example Consider: function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return (

{count}

); } Application starts React ↓ Counter() ↓ count = 0 ↓ React determines UI ↓ DOM is committed ↓ Browser displays 0 User clicks Click ↓ onClick handler ↓ setCount(1) ↓ State update ↓ React schedules work ↓ Counter() runs again ↓ count = 1 ↓ React compares old/new result ↓ Finds

text changed ↓ Commit DOM update ↓ Browser displays 1 That's the entire fundamental React cycle. 21. The terminology cheat sheet 22. The mental model I'd recommend Don't think: "Render means display something on the screen." Instead think: Render = React figures out what the UI should be. Then: Reconciliation = React figures out what changed. Then: Commit = React applies the changes. Then: Paint = the browser displays the result. So the simplified pipeline is: STATE / PROPS CHANGE ↓ RE-RENDER ↓ RECONCILIATION ↓ COMMIT ↓ DOM UPDATED ↓ BROWSER PAINTS ↓ USER SEES UI If you understand that pipeline, terms like useState, useEffect, useMemo, useCallback, and useRef become much easier to understand because you can see exactly where they fit into React's rendering process.

SQL.title: all commands order.docx
SQL.content:
Yes. This is an extremely useful thing to memorize, but there are actually two different orders you should know:
SQL writing/syntax order → the order you type clauses.
SQL logical execution order → the order the database conceptually processes them.
They are not the same.
1. The SQL writing order
For a typical query, think:
SELECT
FROM
JOIN ... ON
WHERE
GROUP BY
HAVING
ORDER BY
LIMIT
So the basic template is:
SELECT columns
FROM table
JOIN other_table
    ON condition
WHERE condition
GROUP BY columns
HAVING aggregate_condition
ORDER BY columns
LIMIT number;
But there are more advanced clauses, so let's build the complete picture.
2. The complete SQL clause order
For a standard SELECT query, the syntax order is roughly:
WITH
SELECT
FROM
JOIN
ON
WHERE
GROUP BY
HAVING
WINDOW
ORDER BY
LIMIT / OFFSET
Not every database supports every clause in exactly the same position, so there are dialect differences.
A very useful MySQL/PostgreSQL-style mental template is:
WITH cte AS (
    ...
)
SELECT ...
FROM ...
JOIN ...
    ON ...
WHERE ...
GROUP BY ...
HAVING ...
ORDER BY ...
LIMIT ...
OFFSET ...;
But there's an important correction:
ON isn't really a standalone clause at the same level as WHERE; it belongs to its JOIN.
Think:
FROM A
JOIN B
    ON A.id = B.id
not:
FROM
JOIN
ON
WHERE
as completely independent pieces.
3. The order you should memorize
I'd recommend memorizing this:
WITH
  ↓
SELECT
  ↓
FROM
  ↓
JOIN + ON
  ↓
WHERE
  ↓
GROUP BY
  ↓
HAVING
  ↓
ORDER BY
  ↓
LIMIT / OFFSET
For most interview questions, this is enough.
But there's a much more important order you should understand.
4. Logical execution order
SQL is written approximately like this:
SELECT
FROM
JOIN
WHERE
GROUP BY
HAVING
ORDER BY
LIMIT
But SQL is logically processed approximately like this:
FROM
  ↓
JOIN / ON
  ↓
WHERE
  ↓
GROUP BY
  ↓
HAVING
  ↓
SELECT
  ↓
DISTINCT
  ↓
ORDER BY
  ↓
LIMIT / OFFSET
This explains a LOT of SQL behavior.
5. Why does this matter?
Consider:
SELECT
    department,
    AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;
You write:
SELECT
FROM
GROUP BY
HAVING
ORDER BY
But conceptually SQL does:
FROM Employees
      ↓
GROUP BY department
      ↓
Calculate AVG(salary)
      ↓
HAVING avg salary > 50000
      ↓
SELECT department, avg_salary
      ↓
ORDER BY avg_salary
This is why SQL has certain restrictions.
6. Let's go clause by clause
Step 1 — WITH
WITH is used for CTEs (Common Table Expressions).
Syntax:
WITH customer_orders AS (
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT *
FROM customer_orders;
Think:
"First, create a temporary named result that my main query can use."
You can have multiple CTEs:
WITH
customer_orders AS (
    ...
),
customer_spend AS (
    ...
),
ranked_customers AS (
    ...
)
SELECT ...
FROM ranked_customers;
7. SELECT
SELECT determines what you want in the final output.
SELECT
    customer_id,
    name,
    salary
FROM Employees;
You can put:
columns
expressions
aggregate functions
CASE
window functions
aliases
calculations
Example:
SELECT
    name,
    salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM Employees;
Important
Even though SELECT is written first, it is not logically processed first.
That's one of the most important SQL concepts.
8. FROM
FROM tells SQL where your initial data comes from.
SELECT *
FROM Employees;
This is the beginning of the logical query.
Think:
"What rows am I working with?"
9. JOIN + ON
Then you bring in other tables.
SELECT
    c.name,
    o.amount
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Think:
"I have my starting rows. What other information do I need?"
10. WHERE
WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation.
SELECT *
FROM Employees
WHERE salary > 50000;
Think:
"Which rows should participate in the rest of the query?"
This distinction is incredibly important.
11. GROUP BY
GROUP BY creates groups.
SELECT
    department,
    AVG(salary)
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department;
Think:
"What does one output group represent?"
For example:
One row per department
        ↓
GROUP BY department
or:
One row per customer
        ↓
GROUP BY customer_id
12. HAVING
HAVING filters groups, not individual rows.
Example:
SELECT
    department,
    AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;
Difference:
WHERE
Filters rows:
WHERE salary > 50000
HAVING
Filters groups:
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000
A very useful interview rule:
WHERE → before GROUP BY
HAVING → after GROUP BY
13. ORDER BY
ORDER BY sorts the final result.
SELECT
    name,
    salary
FROM Employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;
Ascending:
ORDER BY salary ASC;
Descending:
ORDER BY salary DESC;
You can sort by multiple columns:
ORDER BY
    department ASC,
    salary DESC;
Meaning:
Sort departments A → Z, and within each department, highest salary first.
14. LIMIT
LIMIT restricts the number of rows returned.
SELECT *
FROM Employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 5;
Meaning:
Give me the top 5 employees by salary.
In SQL Server, you'll often see:
TOP 5
instead.
PostgreSQL/MySQL commonly use:
LIMIT 5
15. OFFSET
Used to skip rows.
SELECT *
FROM Employees
ORDER BY employee_id
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;
Meaning:
Skip first 20
Take next 10
Useful for pagination.
16. DISTINCT
DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows.
Example:
SELECT DISTINCT department
FROM Employees;
Result:
HR
IT
Finance
Sales
rather than:
IT
IT
IT
HR
HR
Finance
Sales
Sales
Its position is:
SELECT DISTINCT ...
FROM ...
Logically, think of it as happening after the result expressions have been formed and before final ordering/limiting.
17. CASE WHEN
CASE isn't a query clause. It's an expression that can appear in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, etc., depending on the situation.
Example:
SELECT
    name,
    salary,
    CASE
        WHEN salary >= 100000 THEN 'High'
        WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'Medium'
        ELSE 'Low'
    END AS salary_category
FROM Employees;
Think:
"Convert values into categories."
18. Aggregate functions
These are usually used with GROUP BY.
COUNT()
SUM()
AVG()
MIN()
MAX()
Example:
SELECT
    department,
    COUNT(*) AS employee_count,
    AVG(salary) AS avg_salary,
    MAX(salary) AS highest_salary
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department;
Mental flow:
FROM
 ↓
GROUP BY
 ↓
COUNT / SUM / AVG / MAX / MIN
 ↓
SELECT
19. Window functions
This is where things get more advanced.
Examples:
ROW_NUMBER()
RANK()
DENSE_RANK()
LAG()
LEAD()
SUM() OVER()
AVG() OVER()
Example:
SELECT
    employee_id,
    department,
    salary,
    RANK() OVER (
        PARTITION BY department
        ORDER BY salary DESC
    ) AS salary_rank
FROM Employees;
Think:
"I want to calculate something across related rows without collapsing the rows."
That's the key difference between:
GROUP BY
and:
OVER()
GROUP BY
Turns:
10 employees
into:
1 department row
Window function
Keeps:
10 employee rows
but adds information to each row.
20. Window function vs GROUP BY
This is worth memorizing.
GROUP BY
SELECT
    department,
    AVG(salary)
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department;
Output:
IT       70000
HR       60000
Finance  80000
One row per department.
Window function
SELECT
    employee_id,
    department,
    salary,
    AVG(salary) OVER (
        PARTITION BY department
    ) AS dept_avg
FROM Employees;
Output:
1   IT   70000   65000
2   IT   60000   65000
3   HR   60000   58000
4   HR   56000   58000
Employee rows remain.
21. Where does the window function go?
Written syntax:
SELECT
    ...,
    RANK() OVER (...)
FROM ...
WHERE ...
GROUP BY ...
HAVING ...
ORDER BY ...
You generally write window functions in SELECT or ORDER BY.
But conceptually, window functions are evaluated after grouping/aggregation and before the final ordering/limiting.
This explains why you often need a CTE.
Example:
WITH customer_spend AS (
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        SUM(amount) AS total_spend
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT
    customer_id,
    total_spend,
    RANK() OVER (
        ORDER BY total_spend DESC
    ) AS spend_rank
FROM customer_spend;
Mental flow:
Orders
 ↓
GROUP BY customer
 ↓
SUM(amount)
 ↓
customer_spend
 ↓
RANK()
 ↓
final result
22. The full mental model
Here's the one I'd memorize for interviews:
              SQL WRITING ORDER
WITH
 ↓
SELECT
 ↓
FROM
 ↓
JOIN + ON
 ↓
WHERE
 ↓
GROUP BY
 ↓
HAVING
 ↓
ORDER BY
 ↓
LIMIT / OFFSET
But remember:
              SQL LOGICAL ORDER
FROM
 ↓
JOIN + ON
 ↓
WHERE
 ↓
GROUP BY
 ↓
HAVING
 ↓
SELECT
 ↓
WINDOW FUNCTIONS
 ↓
DISTINCT
 ↓
ORDER BY
 ↓
LIMIT / OFFSET
There are some dialect-specific nuances around the exact placement/evaluation of windowing, DISTINCT, and other features, but this is an excellent interview mental model.
23. The biggest interview trap: WHERE vs HAVING
Suppose the question says:
Find departments whose average salary is greater than 50,000.
Wrong:
SELECT
    department,
    AVG(salary)
FROM Employees
WHERE AVG(salary) > 50000
GROUP BY department;
Why?
Because WHERE operates before grouping/aggregation.
Correct:
SELECT
    department,
    AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;
Mental model:
WHERE
"I want these rows"
HAVING
"I want these groups"
24. Another major trap: SELECT alias
Consider:
SELECT
    salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM Employees
WHERE annual_salary > 600000;
This generally doesn't work because WHERE is logically evaluated before the SELECT alias is created.
Instead:
SELECT
    salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM Employees
WHERE salary * 12 > 600000;
Or use a CTE/subquery:
WITH employees AS (
    SELECT
        salary * 12 AS annual_salary
    FROM Employees
)
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE annual_salary > 600000;
This is one reason understanding logical execution order is so useful.
25. Another trap: filtering after LEFT JOIN
Suppose:
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    o.amount
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.amount > 100;
You might think:
"I'm using LEFT JOIN, so I'll get every customer."
But the WHERE condition removes rows where o.amount is NULL.
So the result behaves much more like an inner join for this condition.
Compare:
Condition in WHERE
LEFT JOIN Orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.amount > 100
Condition in ON
LEFT JOIN Orders o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND o.amount > 100
These can produce very different results.
This is a very common SQL interview question.
26. Subquery order
A subquery has its own SQL order.
Example:
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        SUM(amount) AS total_spend
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
) t
WHERE total_spend > 1000;
Outer query:
SELECT
FROM
WHERE
Inner query:
SELECT
FROM
GROUP BY
Think of each query level independently.
27. CTE order
Same idea:
WITH customer_spend AS (
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        SUM(amount) AS total_spend
    FROM Orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT
    customer_id,
    total_spend
FROM customer_spend
WHERE total_spend > 1000
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;
Think:
CTE
 ↓
produces temporary result
 ↓
main query uses it
28. UNION order
For combining result sets:
SELECT customer_id
FROM Customers
UNION
SELECT customer_id
FROM FormerCustomers;
Each SELECT must be compatible.
For example:
same number of columns
compatible data types
You can then order the combined result:
SELECT customer_id
FROM Customers
UNION
SELECT customer_id
FROM FormerCustomers
ORDER BY customer_id;
Generally, the final ORDER BY applies to the combined result.
29. Recursive CTEs
Advanced:
WITH RECURSIVE employees AS (
    -- anchor
    SELECT
        employee_id,
        manager_id,
        name
    FROM Employee
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    -- recursive part
    SELECT
        e.employee_id,
        e.manager_id,
        e.name
    FROM Employee e
    JOIN employees x
        ON e.manager_id = x.employee_id
)
SELECT *
FROM employees;
You don't need to worry about this for basic SQL, but it fits into the WITH portion of your mental model.
30. INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE are different
Everything we've discussed so far is mainly for SELECT.
For DML, memorize separately.
INSERT
INSERT INTO Employees (
    name,
    salary
)
VALUES (
    'John',
    50000
);
Mental structure:
INSERT INTO
 ↓
columns
 ↓
VALUES / SELECT
You can also:
INSERT INTO Employees (name, salary)
SELECT name, salary
FROM TempEmployees;
31. UPDATE
UPDATE Employees
SET salary = salary * 1.10
WHERE department = 'IT';
Order:
UPDATE
 ↓
SET
 ↓
WHERE
Very important: Be careful with UPDATE without WHERE.
UPDATE Employees
SET salary = 0;
That updates every row.
32. DELETE
DELETE FROM Employees
WHERE employee_id = 10;
Order:
DELETE FROM
 ↓
WHERE
Again:
DELETE FROM Employees;
means delete all rows.
33. CREATE TABLE
DDL:
CREATE TABLE Employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100),
    salary DECIMAL(10,2),
    department_id INT
);
Think:
CREATE TABLE
 ↓
columns
 ↓
data types
 ↓
constraints
34. ALTER TABLE
For changing a table:
ALTER TABLE Employees
ADD email VARCHAR(255);
or:
ALTER TABLE Employees
DROP COLUMN email;
or dialect-specific variations for modifying columns/constraints.

36. Your ultimate SQL interview template
When you see a problem, don't immediately start typing.
First think:
1. What does one output row represent?
          ↓
2. Which table gives me those rows?
          ↓
3. Do I need another table?
          ↓
4. Which JOIN?
          ↓
5. Do I filter rows?
          ↓
6. WHERE
          ↓
7. Do I need groups?
          ↓
8. GROUP BY
          ↓
9. Do I filter groups?
          ↓
10. HAVING
          ↓
11. Do I need ranking/comparison?
          ↓
12. Window function
          ↓
13. How should results be sorted?
          ↓
14. ORDER BY
          ↓
15. How many rows?
          ↓
16. LIMIT / OFFSET
And then translate that mental plan into:
WITH ...
SELECT ...
FROM ...
JOIN ...
    ON ...
WHERE ...
GROUP BY ...
HAVING ...
ORDER BY ...
LIMIT ...;
The one line I'd memorize
For SELECT queries:
FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → WINDOW → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
That's the logical thinking order.
And:
WITH → SELECT → FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT
That's the usual writing/syntax order.
If you understand the difference between those two, a huge number of "why doesn't this SQL work?" questions suddenly become much easier.
